A step-by-step build-up of the sequential-selection project: why skipping about 37 % of the candidates is optimal, what changes for small $n$, and where the code and the paper differ.

01Orientation

The project in one screen

Watch the first 37 % of the candidates without committing, then take the first one who beats them all: no other cutoff finds the best candidate more often, and the rule succeeds about 37 % of the time in a long queue, a little more often in a short one.

We see $n$ candidates one by one in random order and must accept or reject each on the spot. The repository states the exact success probability of the cutoff rule, derives the large-$n$ optimum, and checks both by simulation. [[paper:sec:model]] [[code:src/secretary.py:8 def success_probability]]

02Core idea

Skipping candidates buys a benchmark, and the price is that the best may be among them

Start from a sentence: every candidate you skip makes your benchmark better and the chance that the best one is already gone larger. The rule fails in exactly two ways, and the cutoff trades one against the other. The figure shows the trade before the algebra does.

Before you drag: with $n = 20$, does skipping half of the candidates beat skipping a quarter?

No, though only just: 0.359 against 0.366. Both are below the optimum of 0.384 at seven skipped. The curve is flat near its top and falls off steeply only at the extremes.

The same statement, derived

$$\Pn(r) = \frac{r-1}{n} \sum_{k=r}^{n} \frac{1}{k-1}, \qquad r \ge 2 . \tag{1}$$
[[paper:eq:prob]]
$$\win{\Pn(r)} \;\longrightarrow\; \skip{x} \int_{\skip{x}}^1 \frac{dt}{t} \;=\; -\skip{x} \ln \skip{x}$$
$$P'(x) = -\ln \skip{x} - 1 = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \skip{x^\star} = 1/\e, \qquad \win{P(x^\star)} = 1/\e$$
What to keep The optimum balances two failure probabilities, and the same number, $1/\e$, is both the share to skip and the chance of success in the limit. For finite $n$ the success probability lies above $1/\e$ and falls to it, which is why enumerating the exact optimum is worth the three lines of code. Only the first step uses the random arrival order; without that assumption nothing here holds.
03Realization

How the code realizes it, and what the simulation shows

The repository computes the same number twice, once from the formula and once by simulating queues, and the two routes meet only in the results file.

The rule itself is one short function. Look at the comparison in the loop: the first score above the benchmark ends the search, whether or not it is the best. [[code:src/secretary.py:20 def run_once]]

src/secretary.py:20-26the cutoff ruledef run_once(scores: np.ndarray, r: int) -> bool:
    """Apply the rule to one arrival order. True if the overall best candidate is chosen."""
    benchmark = scores[: r - 1].max() if r > 1 else -np.inf
    for s in scores[r - 1:]:
        if s > benchmark:
            return bool(s == scores.max())
    return False  # nobody beat the benchmark: the best was among the skipped candidates

04Honest inventory

What is assumed, what is open, and the notation

Three places where paper, code and results do not say the same thing, one assumption everything rests on, and one open end.

Paper and code answer different questions The paper reports the limit, $x^\star = 1/\e$ with a success probability of 0.368 [[paper:eq:limit]]. The code enumerates the exact optimum for the given $n$ [[code:src/secretary.py:15 def optimal_cutoff]], which gives 0.384 at $n = 20$. Both are right: the finite-$n$ value lies above the limit and falls to it. The simulation section of the paper does not say which of the two its numbers should be compared with. [[paper:sec:sim]]
The code covers a case the paper excludes The paper states the success probability for $r \ge 2$ only [[paper:eq:prob]]. The code returns $1/n$ for $r \le 1$ [[code:src/secretary.py:8 def success_probability]], which is correct (take the first candidate), is stored in the results file, and is drawn as the leftmost point of Figure 3.
Paper and result file disagree For $n = 100$ the results grid moves in steps of five cutoffs, so the best cutoff on the grid is 35 skipped, while the same file stores optimal_r = 38, that is 37 skipped [[result:results/success.json]]. The file is also a single seeded run [[code:src/secretary.py:34 default_rng(7)]], so the agreement in that figure is one draw, not a distribution. A reader of Figure 3 could take the grid maximum for the optimum.
Open question The gap table in section 01 lists payoffs beyond "best or nothing" as planned. Nothing in the code supports a payoff by rank yet, and the single-cutoff derivation above does not carry over to it.
Why the first step needs the random arrival order optional depth

Given that the best candidate stands at position $k$, the first $k-1$ candidates are a uniformly random subset in uniformly random order. The best of them is therefore equally likely to stand at any of the $k-1$ positions, and it stands among the first $r-1$ with probability $(r-1)/(k-1)$. With a trend in quality over time this symmetry fails, and the success probability of the paper with it. [[paper:eq:prob]]
